$comment: Scheduled jobs, declared in one place so a rename cannot silently stop one. Railway's cron is configured in the dashboard per service; this file is the source of truth that tests/config/test_jobs_config.py checks the commands against, and docs/deploy/railway-runbook.md records the dashboard step. `max_silence_minutes` is how long each job may go without a SUCCESSFUL run before app/services/ops/checks.py calls it overdue -- the tolerance is declared here rather than derived from the cron expression, because deriving it needs a cron parser and a parser that mis-reads a schedule produces a monitor that is confidently wrong, which is worse than no monitor. The numbers are the job's own period doubled, with a whole extra period for the frequent jobs (one missed firing of a quarter-hourly job is noise) and six hours on top for the daily ones (long enough for a retry to land, short enough that a day of silence is never normal). tests/ops/test_job_heartbeat.py asserts none of them is shorter than the schedule it guards. **`schedule` is UTC, not Asia/Jerusalem.** Every `why:` below reasons about wall-clock Israel time -- `billing-run` at 08:30, `health-reminders` at 09:30 -- because that is the time a manager or a parent actually reads. Railway's cron reads the five fields as UTC, so for two years every daily job fired three hours later than its own `why:` argues for (verified 2026-09-02, §13.10 of the 2026-09-02 findings register). The five daily, fixed-hour jobs below are shifted by -3h to land on the Jerusalem hour their `why:` names; the `*/15` and hourly jobs are left alone because a periodic schedule fires on the same minutes in any zone. The shift is exact only during Israel Daylight Time (UTC+3, roughly March-October, including 2026-09-02); during Israel Standard Time (UTC+2) every shifted job runs one hour early. That is the accepted cost of a static shift over teaching each worker to read the studio clock -- see tests/config/test_jobs_config.py::test_daily_jobs_fire_at_their_documented_jerusalem_hour.

jobs.name: demo-reset
jobs.why: So the demo data never drifts into a state that hides a bug. 02:00 Asia/Jerusalem is after any evening session a coach might have been testing against. Schedule is UTC (`$comment`): 23:00 UTC lands at 02:00 IDT.

jobs.name: people-followups
jobs.why: The day 1/3/7 ladder is the 7-14 day conversion window every buyer's guide names as decisive; a reminder 24h before the lesson; leads written off after 21 days so the funnel's denominator stays honest; and freeze expiry, because §7 has no unfreeze endpoint and a freeze that never ends leaves a student invisible on every roster while their guardian still reads מוקפא. One job rather than four: they share the same date arithmetic over the same two tables, and four cron entries would be four chances for one to be forgotten. 09:00 Asia/Jerusalem is late enough not to wake anybody and early enough that a parent reads it before the school run. Schedule is UTC (`$comment`): 06:00 UTC lands at 09:00 IDT -- unshifted this ran at noon.

jobs.name: comms-notify
jobs.why: Two passes over the same tables and the same clock, so one entry rather than two: scheduled announcements whose moment has arrived, and the queued-push drain that turns an enqueued notification into a sent one. Every 15 minutes rather than daily, because what this carries is a cancellation — §5.11's own example is ביטול שיעור, היום 17:00, and a message that goes out tomorrow morning is a message that did not go out. §5.12 explicitly rules the calendar feed out as the channel for it ('the feed is for where do I need to be next Tuesday, never for tonight is cancelled'), which leaves this job as the only thing standing between a manager pressing שליחה and a parent's phone buzzing. It is also why the drain is in the same job rather than a slower one: a push that sits queued for a day is §5.11's silent failure with extra steps.

jobs.name: plan-changes
jobs.why: A plan change is scheduled, not immediate: a downgrade takes effect on the first of the month, and something has to move student.price_plan_id and release the future bookings the smaller allowance no longer covers. Upgrades never reach this job -- they apply the moment the parent asks, because withholding access somebody volunteered to pay more for is the worse failure. 02:30 Asia/Jerusalem, after the demo reset and before anybody opens the app: a family whose downgrade lands mid-morning would watch sessions disappear from a screen they were looking at. Daily rather than monthly because `effective_on <= today` is the query -- a day the job does not run must not strand a family on a plan they cancelled. Schedule is UTC (`$comment`): 23:30 UTC lands at 02:30 IDT, still after `demo-reset` at 23:00 UTC.

jobs.name: sessions-complete
jobs.why: The only writer of `session.status = 'completed'`. A session ends by the passage of time and not by anybody doing anything, so nothing in a request path can be responsible for it -- and with no job at all, every class the club has ever held is still `scheduled`, which is what §5.14's 'sessions held vs planned' would have to count. Hourly rather than nightly because the lag IS the wrongness: a nightly pass means every class held today reads as not-yet-happened until tomorrow morning, to a coach looking at the screen twenty minutes after locking up. Hourly rather than every fifteen minutes because sessions are scheduled on clock hours and half-hours, so three of every four passes would update nothing; the query is `ends_at <= now AND status = 'scheduled'` against a composite index, and firing it 96 times a day to catch a 30-minute edge is load bought with nothing. On the hour rather than past it: `ends_at <= at` means a class ending exactly at 18:00 completes at 18:00, which is the boundary the coach is standing at.

jobs.name: billing-run
jobs.why: §5.10's four passes in one daily run: the monthly charge run on the studio's configured run day, the prepayment rung that fires straight after it, the day 3/7/14 debt ladder, and the 24h stale-order sweep. One entry rather than four -- they share the same clock and the same two tables, and the run day is decided inside the job by `studio.settings['billing']['run_day']`, so a cron that tried to encode it would be a second answer to a question the studio already answers. 08:30 Asia/Jerusalem is chosen by two constraints that pin it from both sides. It must be AFTER `plan-changes` at 02:30: a downgrade effective on the 1st has to have moved `student.price_plan_id` before the run bills the month, or the family is billed at the price they cancelled and the refund conversation is the product's fault. And it must be after 08:00, because for the DEBT LADDER the cron hour IS the hour a parent's phone lights up -- `escalate_debt` calls `NotificationService.enqueue` directly, `comms-notify` drains every fifteen minutes -- and, since §13.11, the drain itself now refuses between 21:00 and 08:00 regardless of when the caller enqueued, so a run at 03:00 would queue the message rather than dun a family at 03:15, but 08:30 still keeps the send and the cron hour together rather than relying on that gate to cover for it. 08:30 is the first half hour after the quiet band ends, which also puts the day's charges on `3e` before the office opens. The prepayment rung (`notify_prepay_ending`) is the one pass this argument does NOT have to protect on its own: it also routes through `ReminderService`'s own refusal. That is belt-and-braces, not redundancy that can be dropped -- the ladder still wants a sane cron hour of its own. Schedule is UTC (`$comment`): 05:30 UTC lands at 08:30 IDT, still after `plan-changes` at 23:30 UTC.

jobs.name: health-reminders
jobs.why: §5.5's day 1/3/7 chase for a declaration that has not been signed, plus the renewal pass for the studios that set `health_declaration_validity_months`. Nothing here blocks anything -- §5.5's argument is that blocking a row in an app does not stop a child stepping onto a mat, so chasing the parent is the whole job, and a chase that never runs is §5.5 not implemented. Daily, in waking hours, for the same reason `billing-run` is: this worker enqueues straight through W5's seam and the drain is fifteen minutes behind it, so the cron hour is close to the send hour, and since §13.11 the drain's own quiet-hours gate covers this path too regardless. 09:30 rather than 09:00: `people-followups` already occupies 09:00, and a household that is in both ladders -- a lead being converted whose child has no declaration -- should get two messages far enough apart to read as two, not one buzz containing both. Schedule is UTC (`$comment`): 06:30 UTC lands at 09:30 IDT, thirty minutes after `people-followups` at 06:00 UTC.

jobs.name: attendance-at-risk
jobs.why: Register §2.3 -- `attendance.at_risk` was fully specified (kinds.py, both apps' AtRiskAlert) and nothing produced it; this is the producer. Daily rather than on every mark, because §5.14's rule is about a PATTERN across several sessions, not a single tap -- computing it at write time would fire mid-cycle on marks a coach is still correcting, and computing it on every dashboard read would repeat the same streak-walk query for every manager who opens the card. 07:00 Asia/Jerusalem, before `people-followups` and `health-reminders` occupy 09:00 and 09:30: most marking happens the evening before, so the streak for last night's session is already settled by morning, and a manager opening the dashboard at breakfast sees the freshest count the day can offer rather than one still catching up to yesterday evening. Idempotent per streak (not per run) via `streak_start_session_id` in the notification payload -- see the worker's own docstring for why a job that re-fired on every unchanged streak would be the failure §5.11's whole fan-out exists to avoid. Schedule is UTC (`$comment`): 04:00 UTC lands at 07:00 IDT, still ahead of `people-followups` at 06:00 UTC.

jobs.name: privacy-requests
jobs.why: Drains the §11.3 export and §11.4 deletion queues. Hourly because these are the only jobs here a person is watching a status screen for: a guardian who asks for their child's data is owed movement, and a request that sits `pending` overnight reads as a product that ignored them. There is no retry storm in a frequent schedule -- each pass takes only `status = 'pending'`, so a request that resolves either way is never picked up twice. At :20 to keep it clear of `sessions-complete` on the hour. **Both halves currently refuse on purpose.** `assemble_export_bundle` and `purge_subject_data` raise `NotImplementedError`, and this job's real work today is turning a request into `failed` with a reason a human can read. That is deliberate: before it was scheduled the stub would have marked a §11.4 erasure request `completed` having deleted nothing, and unlike the export -- which PostgreSQL rejects via `(status = 'completed') = (object_key IS NOT NULL)` -- no constraint can be written that checks data is gone. Scheduling it is what makes the gap visible on a screen instead of invisible behind a queue nobody drains.

jobs.name: ops-check
jobs.why: Evaluates every check in app/services/ops/checks.py and emails when the set of failing ones has GROWN since the last email. `environment: all` and not one named environment, which is the only entry in this file to use it: a monitor that exists in one environment and not another is the same defect it was built to catch, and staging is where this product actually runs today while production is still unpopulated. Every fifteen minutes because that is the cadence of `comms-notify`, the job whose silence is the most expensive here -- a monitor slower than the thing it watches turns a missed cancellation into a two-hour gap before anybody is told. Growth rather than any-red is what makes that cadence bearable: a job broken over a weekend is one email rather than two hundred and eighty-eight, and the two hundred and eighty-ninth would be filtered into a folder along with the next real one. **This job cannot detect its own silence.** If it stops running, nothing mails -- the same failure one level up. Its own heartbeat is on the platform console like every other job's, which makes the gap visible to somebody who looks; closing it properly needs a pinger outside the box, which is exactly the vendor that was deliberately not bought. Stated here rather than left to be discovered.
